title: How Fatih Akin Breathed Life Into San Sebastian’s Haunting Opener ‘Ghost Song’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 18, 2026 4:00am 'Ghost Song' San Sebastian Film Festival Fatih Akin is no stranger to the festival circuit, having wowed Berlin with his Golden Bear-winning Head-On in 2004 and nabbing best screenplay in Cannes for The Edge of Heaven in 2007. The German-Turkish filmmaker, also a Golden Globe winner for 2017’s In the Fade , has sent a couple of movies to San Sebastian over the years. “I don’t remember which films it was,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter on Zoom. “But I always wanted to go.” Akin is getting his chance and then some with this year’s haunting opener Ghost Song , following two students who meet in a Berlin nightclub and immediately fall head over heels in love. Farasha (Mariam Dawoud) and Faris (Eren M. Güvercin) are struck by a deep-rooted connection that they can’t wait to untangle, but the cord is abruptly cut short when Farasha is killed. For the next 40 nights, she visits Faris in his dreams, where their mutual infatuation slowly drives him to the brink of insanity. Related Stories Movies Tokyo Film Festival Unveils Gala and Anime Selections, Featuring Cate Blanchett, Tony Gilroy, 'Wild Horse Nine' and 'Grotesqqque' Movies Alfonso Cuarón to Make First Korea Visit for Busan Film Festival The Warner Bros. film, co-written with Ruth Toma and set for release in Germany Nov. 5, is actually inspired by Akin’s own discovery of anime and manga, and bolstered by his desire to make Ghost Song for a younger audience. “I’m not a boomer, but I’m Generation X, and Gen Z is very different,” he says. “They work with very different tools and worlds, and you have this influence [that] is not coming from Hollywood. You have this influence coming from Asia, from Japan, China, Korea.” The black-and-white feature is both tender and harrowing, the anime influence palpable in the beautifully illustrated title cards marking the remaining nights Farasha and Faris have together. The story also deftly draws on spirituality rooted in the Islamic tradition — a nod to Akin’s religious upbringing. “It’s my form of dealing with that,” he tells THR , “or using it as storytelling.” Below, ahead of its glitzy red carpet premiere on Friday as Spain’s most prestigious film festival officially gets underway, Akin unpacks the making of Ghost Song . He talks about its depiction of teen suicides — “everybody knows somebody in the generation of my kids who [took their own life] or who tried to” — as well as his decision to keep the film in black-and-white, its similarity to Demi Moore and Patrick Swayze’s Ghost , and why he’s vowed to never relive this particular process again: “This is the very last time I do it this way.” When did this journey start, and why this story? It all started about 10 years ago. It was basically an idea [from] my son. He had this idea of me doing a film for kids, and it was a story about two friends, and one is a ghost — two boys and they’re best friends. I liked the idea of doing something for children, which was very different than what I did before. And I gave it to this writer, Ruth Toma, who I had worked with before. And she wrote the screenplay for this children’s movie. But then I turned to doing In the Fade and other stuff. We never stopped developing the screenplay in the meantime. And what happened was, with the growing up of my children, the age of the characters had changed. That happened [naturally], and so the focus shifted as well and it became a romantic [film]. My kids really taught me or showed me the world of anime. I was very much in manga and graphic novels before… But I was wondering, can I combine it with my take on cinema? So there’s an anime influence on this film? Very much. Anime films often have this romantic touch. They are in this fantasy world, you know? Like parallel universes, rebirth, dying and coming back — this is very popular in the anime world. But also social matters. A Silent Voice is a film about mobbing and suicide in the teenage world or in the young adult world, and so anime is a tool or a window for a younger generation than I am. I’m not a boomer, but I’m Generation X, and Gen Z is very different. They work with very different tools and worlds, and you have this influence [that] is not coming from Hollywood. You have this influence coming from Asia, from Japan, China, Korea. I was very much influenced by Western cinema, by American cinema. Filmmaker Fatih Akin at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival. Courtesy of Getty Are there any particular directors from that region that you’re a fan of? Hayao Miyazaki, the guy who won the Academy Award with Spirited Away . All his work is pretty influential, and of course, the guys who made Suzume , Your Name and Belle , these are incredible pieces of work, in a very visual way. I had the opportunity to do [that] with this film: combine it with that world [and make] a spiritual film. When you think about spiritual films, you end up with Kundun or The Last Temptation of Christ stuff, but I see more the desire and need of doing such a film for a director. Spirituality, the supernatural… I’m interested in this stuff in a private way, but how can you make a film about it that’s still for a wider audience? Ghost Song gave me the opportunity to do that — to do a spiritual film, but to do it as much [for]… I don’t know. Pop culture. It’s interesting that this started as a children’s film because it really is quite morbid. It’s not a children’s film anymore. It started as a children’s film, but then it became […] [for] young adults. And what we found out when we worked on this is that suicide is the highest reason for dying between 15 to 25-year-olds in the whole world. I didn’t know that, and it was scary. Suicide is a theme which has always popped up in my work. I don’t know why these things pop up in my work, but it’s here [in Ghost Song ] again. And everybody knows somebody in the generation of my kids who [took their own life] or who tried to. COVID was a very depressing period for this generation. So I observe that, in a way. I deal with that. I think the film is for everybody in a way — not too young — but sometimes I can understand that people of 60 years, if they don’t have kids or if their kids are grown up, that they cannot connect with such a film. But a younger audience can. And I’m 53 now. I’m thinking about getting old, and to do such a film and to connect with a younger audience… It keeps me young. ( Laughs. ) This film tackles so much: suicide, mental health, young love. I want to ask about the mythology of this film, if that’s the right word. The lore, and Farasha haunting Faris for 40 nights. Is that rooted in a certain tradition? Yes, the Islamic tradition. But we discovered that Orthodox Christianity has that too. […] I have this Islamic background. I grew up in an Islamic family, a very faithful, religious family. It’s my form of dealing with that, or using it as storytelling. It was beautiful. I don’t know if I saw the final version of the film — I saw a black and white version? That is the final version. I have two versions. That happened because the anime world was influencing this film, so when you do a film, you have reference films. The only reference films I had for this one, which I gave to my DP, were the anime films. Your Name , A Silent Voice , maybe Ghost , the Patrick Swayze film. ( Laughs .) But nothing else on a visual level comes to mind. So this was the influence, and the colors and the color grading was very important. For the first time, I really, really, really worked with strong colors. It starts with the costume and goes through the set design and the lighting, but very much the grading as well. And the grading is a process in filmmaking that comes at the end, after the film is edited and done. [But] with the fast rush and to not get distracted by it or not lose the faith in the visuality of the material, what did I do? I switched off the colors in the editing process. And what happened is we got used to it. The whole film was a long journey and very difficult to edit. I was in the editing room [for] almost six months. What do you do when you edit six months in black and white? You get used to it, and that’s like a relationship. You fall in love with it. So [we were] like, “Okay, let’s keep it in black and white.” It’s beautiful in black and white, and it’s existential in black and white. And this film is about existentialism, and it’s manga, and manga and anime are in black and white because the colors are too expensive to print. It became this art form. It’s so strong and so unique. So which one will you screen in San Sebastian? The black and white. I’m asking that they also show a color version of the film. I’m not sure if I have convinced the festival committee yet. But we have the opening in black and white, and I hope that I can get a second screening in color because you have to see both versions of the film to have the complete picture. This is also very much an immigrant story. And we see glimpses of Farasha’s journey to Europe. I wanted to ask whether that’s rooted in anything personal for you? I am always looking for heroines and heroes who are not that common in Western cinema, but [are] part of the Western world when you go out on the street. I’ve always done that since my very first film. I don’t know if it’s just personal. It’s something I observe on the street in daily life. Syrian migration in Germany since 2015 has become very visible in Germany, and these people somehow adapted to so much and so fast, as well. I mean, they’re in the medical sector and the care sector. They’re in all sectors, and they changed this country. The Turks have been here since the ’60s of the last century, but the Syrians came 10 years ago. It was an opportunity to put that in the story as well. To give more texture. I don’t have these typical rock-and-roll kids [as] heroes. Faith is important for [Farasha] in a way. Maybe her faith, her religion, makes her otherworldly. You have to believe in that… If you deal with life and death and past life, you automatically end up in a spiritual film, and so it was a way or an opportunity to use my personal biography in this spirituality of the film. How do you hope the audience reacts after watching Ghost Song ? I’ve seen some reactions [already]. Some reactions really shocked me — some people, they’re very much emotionally shaken by the film. I had never seen that before, or in other works I did. Usually, it’s not so much a young audience who’s like that. It’s more like 30 and up, you know? For them, this is a roller coaster, and I always try to give the audience a physical experience as well. I think if a film reaches a physical level — laughing, crying, whatever it is… If this two-dimensional medium can create that, can create goosebumps, but on the other hand, console. […] I hope this film could be a friend for a lot of young people. It deals with life and death, but in a life-positive way. It’s a tragic love story — we don’t have that too much these days in the cinema, especially a lot in German cinema. It’s catharsis. It’s a troubled world. Everybody has a lot of issues all over the world, and you get sidetracked from that escapism. If a film can give you catharsis, it can be very helpful. What does it mean to be opening the San Sebastian Film Festival ? It’s my first time at San Sebastian [Film Festival]. I think in the past, I sent films there and they passed [on them]. I don’t remember which films it was. But I always wanted to go to San Sebastian. It has that great name and good food and [it’s a] sophisticated festival in a way. I was very, very curious always about that because I have a lot of friends in Spain, and I think I have an audience in Spain, so I have a good relationship [with] that country. To get to that festival with this film and opening it, it means a lot to me. It’s also good to know that there aren’t just the usual suspects to present a film. I mean, Cannes is great, and it did a lot for me. And so did Venice and Berlin. But there are other parts of the world, other festivals in the world. It’s not just that I want to support them, but they also support you. I feel very humble and and very honored that they picked up the film for opening. You know, in [the World Cup], I wanted Spain to win. ( Laughs. ) How were you able to get Ghost Song funded? We got government funding. But our biggest supporter, and I’m very thankful that I have them, was Warner Brothers. [Around] half of the budget is coming from Warner Brothers., I’m not sure. My producers know it better. ( Laughs. ) It was very difficult to finance this film. Very, very, very difficult. On the one hand, films have become more and more and more expensive, especially in Germany. That’s why a lot of German filmmakers move somewhere else to do their films. The cost, everything gets so high here. And you never get the full budget for any film. Here, and also for [my] last two films, [including Cannes-premierer] Amrum , we went into the risk. We said, “Okay, we are not [at] full budget,” but we still greenlit the film. This is becoming more and more dangerous. This is the very last time I do it this way. Life is too short. It’s heart attacks and cortisol and sleepless nights! It’s not like when I started doing films. I was this young filmmaker in another time, in another country. You had some kids, you had some employees and a company and you’d do a film and fulfill that. It doesn’t work like that anymore. As someone who has been working with Warner Bros. recently, and with a lot of European creatives speaking about the proposed Paramount takeover, can I ask: do you have an opinion? Nobody knows. As a rule in filmmaking, nobody knows shit. And I don’t know about tomorrow. […] I don’t have an opinion about that. I can just say I work with the team in Germany and the U.K., and they’re very supportive. I have to say, a brilliant, professional, great team, and a lot of fun to work with. This interview has been shortened and edited for clarity. The 2026 San Sebastian International Film Festival runs Sep. 18-26. THR

title: Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’
full_text: Sep 18, 2026 3:37am PT Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Japan’s Top Broadcasters Unite for First Joint Delegation to MipCancun (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ 3 hours ago ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ 5 hours ago See All Toronto Film Festival “ The Age of Goodbyes ” begins, in more ways than one, with a curse. In Li Zi Shu’s sprawling Malaysian Chinese novel, a family is said to be marked by early death; in Edmund Yeo ‘s screen adaptation, in the Special Presentations section of the Toronto Film Festival , that curse becomes the hinge on which five decades of Malaysian history swing, carried by a woman named Du Li An and the two men, one thought dead, who share the same face. Related Stories Jordan Firstman, Matteo Lane Lead U.S. Voice Cast of Cannes Breakout Comedy 'Jim Queen’ (EXCLUSIVE) Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: 'We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us' (EXCLUSIVE) Li Zi Shu’s book, which begins on page 513 as a deliberate nod to May 13, 1969, was long considered too structurally slippery for cinema, its timelines folding into one another, its narrators unreliable, its boundary between memory and myth left permanently uncertain. That date refers to race riots that broke out in Kuala Lumpur following a bitterly contested general election, leaving hundreds dead and prompting a state of emergency; the ethnic and political fault lines that hardened in its aftermath still shape Malaysia today. Popular on Variety “I wasn’t interested in taking this very labyrinthine novel and making everything neat and chronological for the audience,” Yeo tells Variety . “I wanted to find a cinematic equivalent for the experience of reading it.” Even the novelist had her doubts. “In fact, when I first met Li Zi Shu to discuss the project, her first question to me was, ‘Are you sure it is adaptable?'” Yeo recalls. He told her then that he knew he could not reproduce the novel literally. At the center of the frame story is Kai (Troy Liu), a boy who stumbles onto a novel titled “The Age of Goodbyes” and finds himself drawn into the world of Du Li An ( Vivian Sung ), whose romance with Lin Sang (Stanley Yau) in Ipoh in 1969 ends when he vanishes after confiding in her about his family’s curse. Years later, a man named Mong Sang, also played by Yau, arrives bearing Lin Sang’s exact face and insisting he is someone else entirely. The film, a Taiwan-Malaysia co-production shot in Mandarin, Cantonese, Malay, Thai and English, marks Yeo’s fifth fiction feature, following “River of Exploding Durians,” “We, the Dead,” “Malu” and “Moonlight Shadow.” Yeo made one significant departure from the source material. In the novel, Lin Sang disappears on the day Du Li An marries another man, Steely Bo; in the film, Yeo tied that disappearance directly to the racial violence of May 13 instead. “They are ordinary people living inside history, and its consequences are felt through fear, absence, separation, rumors, memories and things people don’t say,” he says. That instinct comes from Yeo’s own family. He discovered Li Zi Shu’s novel shortly after a trip to China, where he visited his family’s ancestral shrine in Chaoshan and learned new details about his grandfather’s migration to Southeast Asia. His mother once told him that his great-grandfather was a kung fu master who leapt across a moving train while carrying his infant grandson to safety, a story he has no way of confirming. “I think families are full of stories like this,” he says. “Someone tells a story, someone else remembers it slightly differently, certain details disappear while others become more dramatic, and eventually nobody is around anymore who can tell you what actually happened.” That inheritance runs through the soundtrack, too. Several songs in the film were written and performed by Yeo’s own parents in the 1970s, decades before their son thought to build a movie around a fictional Ipoh where they might have been playing on the radio. “The whole film is about things being transmitted from one generation to another: stories, memories, trauma, myths, even gestures,” Yeo says. “And suddenly my mother’s actual voice, singing a song composed by my father and recorded when they were young, was being transmitted through a film I was making decades later.” For Sung, the challenge was finding continuity in a character who ages from a lovestruck young woman into a wife, mother and stepmother across shifting timelines and an uncertain grip on her own past. “When I first spoke with the director about the script, he told me that Du Li An was a ‘survivor.’ That word stayed with me and became the key to understanding her,” Sung says. Playing opposite Yau as both the vanished Lin Sang and his double, Mong Sang, meant sitting inside uncertainty rather than resolving it. Sung recalls filming Du Li An’s first sight of Mong Sang. “My mind was telling me very clearly, ‘This isn’t him.’ But my body and my memories believed something else,” she says. That confusion is written into the dialogue itself. Du Li An speaks Cantonese at home, Mandarin with Lin Sang and Cantonese with Mong Sang. “Sometimes, when she speaks Mandarin with Mong Sang, it actually reveals that the person she is really trying to speak to is Lin Sang,” Sung says. Sung, who is Taiwanese, spent five to six months preparing the role, working with two language coaches on a 1960s Malaysian Chinese Cantonese and Hokkien accent and living for a month in Kuala Lumpur before joining the crew for pre-production in Ipoh. The costume department let her keep the qipaos she wore in fittings. “There was this strong feeling that I wasn’t simply wearing a costume. It felt like my body had somehow stepped into another era,” she says. Yeo built the film’s structure around a delayed reveal: the title card does not appear until 40 minutes in, marking the point where the novel itself begins. Everything before it, he says, is his own expansion of material only briefly suggested on the page, an approach he traces back to adapting Banana Yoshimoto’s novella “Moonlight Shadow.” “What ‘Moonlight Shadow’ gave me was confidence that adaptation is ultimately a conversation with the original work,” Yeo says. “You have to identify its soul rather than protect every incident.” Sung, who relocated from Taiwan to Los Angeles two years ago, isn’t chasing a specific type of role next. She’s drawn to a story about modern love. “Two people who really like each other, but both come with their own problems, fears, and maybe a little bit of craziness,” she says. Yeo is already developing several new projects, among them a century-spanning vampire story set between Borneo, Macau and Kaohsiung, and a multigenerational drama connecting Malaysia and Japan through a family of filmmakers. “Apparently, after making a film about people being haunted by stories from the past, I responded by developing several more films about people being haunted by stories from the past,” he says. title: “This Is So Uncomfortable”: Douglas Booth on Putting Britain’s Police Misogyny Problem on TV
full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 18, 2026 3:00am Douglas Booth in 'The Blame' Courtesy of ITV Logo text Douglas Booth has, admittedly, always been drawn to rather eccentric characters. The English star has been in this business for almost two decades — “so old now,” he laughs over Zoom, mussing up a famously good head of hair — and in that time has portrayed rock stars ( The Dirt ), poets ( Mary Shelley ) and fairies ( The Sandman ). “It’s really hard to go and play Boy George or Nikki Sixx or Dan Leno,” Booth tells The Hollywood Reporter . “Certain actors can’t do that, but I thrive on that.” As thrilling as thriving is, Booth, who was undoubtedly part of an unofficial 2010s “Brit Pack” of 20-something actors with his Riot Club co-stars Sam Claflin and Max Irons, found himself gunning for a part that would involve less fantasy and more familiarity. “I very much love playing people that are just so far removed from myself,” he says. “[But] this was a good time to play a modern bloke. Does that sound silly?” Related Stories Movies Tokyo Film Festival Unveils Gala and Anime Selections, Featuring Cate Blanchett, Tony Gilroy, 'Wild Horse Nine' and 'Grotesqqque' Movies Alfonso Cuarón to Make First Korea Visit for Busan Film Festival The product of Booth’s self-set challenge to take on “normalcy” is anything but silly. In ITV ‘s six-episode The Blame , premiering Sept. 20, he stars as Tom, a detective in a run-of-the-mill English town trying to be a good guy. His professional partner, Emma ( Michelle Keegan ), is a headstrong presence in the force and consistently confronts the everyday sexism that permeates the office. But a teenage ice-skater’s murder soon draws Emma and Tom down a dark, twisty path, forcing them to investigate their own team. In what will almost certainly shock viewers tuning into The Blame , adapted from Charlotte Langley’s book of the same name, the show depicts actual text messages from the real-life Metropolitan Police group chat scandals, in which multiple investigations exposed deep-rooted and systemic racism, homophobia and sexism — dismissed as “banter” — poisoning the country’s top police force. Such was Booth’s discomfort finding out these texts were sent by U.K. police officers that he felt confident The Blame could send Brits an important message. “I remember reading [and thinking], ‘No woman would ever [write this]. This is just so uncomfortable and shocking.’ And then, yes, on the script, it came up: ‘These are all real text messages from members of the Met Police who’ve now been dismissed,'” he recalls to THR . “It lands really well in this series and anchored it for me. It’s also the reason why we’re making a big commercial series that, I felt, is one of the first to really delve into the problems we have with misogyny in the police force.” Below, Booth discusses what he hopes The Blame can achieve and why Tom is caught “in a moral bear trap.” He also touches on the career he’s built, the U.K.’s adoration of a gripping police procedural and whether he’d ever be up for playing a particular fictional spy dominating a lot of the current headlines: “I would sound disingenuous if I said that playing such an iconic character wouldn’t appeal to me.” I know this story is adapted from a book. Did you know much about it before the show came up? I didn’t know anything about the book. I got a message from my agent and a message from [Quay Street Productions] founder Nicola Shindler, who’s an amazing producer. I’d actually worked with her on my first-ever lead performance when I played Boy George [in Worried About the Boy ]. She [sent] an email saying, “You may remember me,” which I very much did. I had an amazing experience working with her before. I mean, she’s been nominated for like 13 BAFTAs or something ridiculous. So instantly, my ears pricked up. And then I read the script and absolutely loved it. I stupidly read it right before I went to bed, and then I couldn’t get to sleep because of the twist at the end of episode one. And I was like, “What?!” It really was a page-turner. I also think it had something important to say. From the beginning of episode one, I was immediately suspicious of a couple of characters. At its core, it’s a whodunit set within a police station, right? But you will be guessing until the very end of the last episode. Everyone comes under suspicion at some point for different reasons. One could call them red herrings, but I don’t necessarily think they are. It’s the fun of watching a thriller — if you’re sat there watching something like, ‘I think it’s that [person], or that [person].’ It’s quite a complex story with a lot of things going on. As you get into it, there is a tangled web of things that all get resolved the right way, but everything that happens happens for a reason. You’ll find out more about Tom and Emma’s past and how they’ve leaned on each other. British star Douglas Booth says he liked the idea of playing “a modern bloke.” Yellow Belly Photo How would you describe Tom as a character for audiences coming into this show? He is a man very much trapped between two worlds . Ultimately, Tom is someone who wants to be a good person. He’s got himself trapped in this toxic work culture, and he’s very much trying to do the right thing. But along the way, he’s probably got himself into a bit of a moral injury and made some compromised decisions — as does Emma, as do many people in that department. In my head, when I was playing him, I kind of imagined that he’d got his foot stuck in a moral bear trap, and he just couldn’t quite get himself free. He’s wrestling with that, and it’s corroding his internal core a little bit. To take a step back and [give] an outside view of Tom, he’s a detective at this police station. He’s very close with Emma. I feel, in certain ways, he feels isolated from the rest of the department. He’s in a constant wrestle with his principles, but also his ambition and drive to be promoted and do well in life… His eggs are very much all in one basket. And sometimes I feel that about myself in this career. ( Laughs .) All my eggs are very much in this basket. I always try to understand the humanity behind it, you know […] if you find out something compromising that could derail the whole thing right before you get across the finish line — do you say something or do you not say something? It was that wrestling with inner human greed and the want to progress alongside your principles. I read that this series uses the actual text messages from multiple real-life cases of toxic police group chat scandals in the U.K. Were you shocked when you found that out? That is one of the most shocking moments of the series, apart from some of the twists and turns towards the end, and probably the most sickening. It’s absolutely awful, and it’s really shocking. And I was like, “I can’t believe [the show writers] have written this.” I remember reading [and thinking], ‘This can’t be no writer… no woman would ever [write this]. This is just so uncomfortable and shocking.’ And then, yes, on the script, it came up: “These are all real text messages from members of the Met Police who’ve now been dismissed.” It lands really well in this series and again, it anchored it for me. It’s also the reason why we’re making a big commercial series that, I felt, is one of the first to really delve into the problems we have with misogyny in the police force. When we were filming, it was the [BBC] Panorama Charing Cross film [about the] WhatsApp group — it came out the year we were shooting. It is shocking and disgusting behavior. You can’t quite believe the misogynistic, racist things that these people are saying. [The show] very much reflects the problems that we have with some of our systems and institutions, the police that are supposed to be protecting us that are potentially letting us — and specifically women — down. Is the hope very much among writers and producers of this show that The Blame prompts discussion and stays with viewers? As you said, it’s a big commercial series, so hopefully a lot of eyeballs on a very important story. I hope so. First and foremost, it’s a gripping thriller about a murder, and then it quickly becomes more complex. I think we obviously want the themes of the show to stay with people, and I think hopefully by the end of the series they will have. But yeah, there were definitely conversations about it, and there was a lot of sharing. I was always sending the producer the constant BBC News headlines about the failure of the police. But at the same time, I also have a lot of respect for the police. It’s a really difficult job that they do. So the aim definitely wasn’t to go out there and be police bashing in in any way. They do a really tricky job, but there are systematic failings that just don’t seem to be fully addressed. We’d be thrilled if it started a conversation or at least made however many of the — hopefully — millions of people that watch it… If it makes a small amount of them, particularly men who have acted inappropriately or [people who] have been acted inappropriately upon, to sit up and think about their position within that, then could only be a very good thing. It was refreshing to see all of this explored through such a strong character in Emma. Have you and Michelle crossed paths before? No, I’ve literally never crossed paths with Michelle before, which is rare because I’ve been doing this almost two decades. So old now. ( Laughs. ) Over half my life. But yeah, she’s famously one of the nicest people in the industry. I’ve only heard incredible things, and she’s the nation’s sweetheart. When you’re around her, people just love her wherever you go — from all walks of life. She’s so grounded and down-to-earth. And we just got on like a house on fire. Also, she’s not in loads of things. She’s in things that run for a while. She’s in good things. It was a real pleasure to work with her and that really helped our chemistry throughout the series. Michelle Keegan and Douglas Booth for ‘The Blame’ ITV You have been in this industry, as you say, for nearly two decades. I think I first saw you in Great Expectations or The Riot Club , over a decade ago. How does The Blame capture this chapter of your career and which roles are talking to you at the moment? It sounds silly to say but it was the chance to play a very normal person — to play a detective my own age in a six-part show where I could really just explore that human element and that complex character. That was a real draw for me. The job I just did before, I played a fairy in The Sandman for years, so I’d been getting up, having prosthetic ears put on my face at 3.30 every morning. When you’re younger, you try to pretend that you have some great master plan for your career, making choices like you’re Leonardo DiCaprio. But not everyone is blessed like Leonardo DiCaprio to work with Martin Scorsese from the age of 20 or whatever. You’re always trying to do the best work that’s available to you. And this was a really exciting script, with a producer I really trusted, and Michelle was great. […] You make independent movies and you go to film festivals and 150 people see them and that’s it. ( Laughs .) So I guess if there was any strategic thinking in the choice, it was to be in a commercial show that had lots of eyeballs on it and just play a man. I’m often drawn to playing fairies or rock stars or poets. I love playing musical performers like in The Limehouse Golem and I very much love playing people that are just so far removed from myself. This was a good time to play a modern bloke. Does that sound silly? Not at all. It’s really hard to go and play Boy George or Nikki Sixx or Dan Leno. Certain actors can’t do that, but I thrive on that. And I think it was a challenge for me, for over a good six-hour stretch, to just play a bloke. I want to ask about The Sandman and the Netflix of it all. At this moment, in an industry with a very saturated market, where the streamers are dominating and the broadcasters are a little more cash-strapped, the police procedural continues to do very well. Can you speak a little bit about that and why they’re so important here? It’s funny you say the traditional broadcasters are more cash-strapped, but when you do this show [ The Blame ], I can’t walk through the city without being on a 30-foot-high billboard in every single train station. If [the broadcasters] think they’ve got a good horse, they’ll back it, and then you make a massive Netflix show, and they don’t do a single bit of promotion for it because they don’t feel they have to. So the way they spend the money is quite interesting. On the importance of it, I can only answer it from my own experience of doing this and having one coming out, but the amount of people that want to talk to me about it or are excited for it in my day-to-day life… My mates don’t normally give a crap about anything I’m in. ( Laughs .) That’s why I love it. They couldn’t care less whether I’m in this movie or doing that, but the amount of people who say, “I can’t wait to watch [ The Blame ].” There’s something about it. I don’t know whether it’s going back to school, that autumn feeling. It’s pure comfort food [in] entertainment. A quick note on what you’ve got coming up: The Way of the Wind . Can we talk about that? That’s a Terrence Malick movie. I filmed it a couple of years ago now. It was a really beautiful moment in time. My agent said, “Oh, Terrence Malick wants to speak to you. You need to call his assistant.” I called his assistant and got through to Terrence and he said, “Oh, Douglas, it’s so great to speak to you. I don’t think I’ve seen you since you were on stage with McKellen…” I was like, ‘This is all a mistake. They think I’m someone else! I’ve told my friends I’m going to do a Terrence Malick film.’ And I said, “I don’t think I was born then, Terrence. [You’re] talking to Douglas Booth.” And he was like, “Oh, Douglas. I thought I was talking to Douglas Hodge,” who he’d also offered a part in the film to. Luckily, it wasn’t a mistake. He’s seen the Mary Shelley movie I made with Elle Fanning and my wife, Bel Powley. I can’t actually say too much, but that film made him want me to play a part in this film. I would love to see it, but he’s been editing it for a very long time. He is an absolutely wonderful man to work with. He didn’t sit down once on set — he’s always by the camera, still like a young child, still so hungry, and communicates with you through old, typewriter-print letters. He’s so inquisitive. Apart from Terrence, do you have a dream director you’d like to work with? You’ve already done so much, so I also have to ask: Bond? Does that appeal? You’re in the right age range and you’re British. ( Laughs .) I would sound disingenuous if I said that playing such an iconic character wouldn’t appeal to me. But I’m definitely not the one making the decisions on whether I will or not. I’d love to work with Denis Villeneuve. He’s fantastic. Paul Thomas Anderson, Quentin Tarantino, if he ever makes movies again. Chris Nolan. I’m saying very basic answers! I’ve worked with Darren Aronofsky and the Wachowskis and when you work with these filmmakers who make such big, iconic movies, there is a thrill about it. The Blame premieres in the U.K. on ITV Sept. 20. THR

title: ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’
full_text: Sep 18, 2026 1:41am PT ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Japan’s Top Broadcasters Unite for First Joint Delegation to MipCancun (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ 2 hours ago ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ 4 hours ago See All Netflix Competitive Bollywood fusion dance has thrived on American college campuses for decades, but it has rarely been the subject of a scripted feature film. Lena Khan ‘s “ Best of the Best ,” premiering Friday on Netflix , follows childhood best friends Maya and Anjali as they join UCLA’s competitive dance team, only to discover that the road to the U.S. Championship is far more raucous and cutthroat than they imagined. Related Stories EbonyLife's Mo Abudu on TIFF Premiere 'The Secret Lives of Baba Segi's Wives' and 'the Consequences of the Decisions We Take as Women' TIFF Takeaways: A Chris Rock Crowd-Pleaser, Peter Farrelly's 'Rocky' Standing Ovation and Market Growing Pains Written by Hasan Minhaj and Prashanth Venkataramanujam, who each competed in similar circuits growing up, the script drew Khan in even though she was not initially sure she would take on the project. Early on, she recalls mentioning it to a childhood friend, who was dismissive. “Bollywood competitions, really?” the friend said, and made it seem like it was not that cool, according to Khan, who says the reaction reflects something broader. “I think South Asians, especially in the diaspora, are so used to not even having our own self-respect.” Popular on Variety That realization shaped how she approached the film’s tone. “We have so much respect for the skill sets of other cultures. We’re looking at kung fu, we’re looking at these different arts. But when we look at our own, we’re used to seeing ourselves as Apu or as the funny nerdy side characters,” Khan says. She wanted the movie to carry a different posture entirely. “We can be proud of things that we do as South Asians,” she says. Minhaj and Venkataramanujam drew on their own backgrounds for the script. Minhaj’s wife danced competitively, and Venkataramanujam performed with an a cappella team called Chai Town, giving him firsthand knowledge of how consuming the competition circuit can become. Khan spent time with UCLA’s own dance team and traveled to North Carolina to observe competitions in preparation. Khan’s earlier work directing episodes of Netflix’s “Never Have I Ever” fed into how she thinks about representation. “When you have more than one of a minority character, then there’s suddenly become real characters,” she says, describing the shift that happens once side characters are allowed the same depth as anyone else. “You get to focus on the humanity between them, the things that become relatable to everybody else.” Casting required actors who could carry both comedy and depth, and several, including Maitreyi Ramakrishnan, had never danced competitively before landing their roles. Khan recalls pushing Ramakrishnan toward a specific physical transformation during casting. “I need you to give me some Channing Tatum energy. And then I was like, no, actually, I need you to do a Christian Bale on me. I need a complete athletic transformation,” she says. Ramakrishnan went on to complete months of intensive dance training ahead of the shoot. Khan built the dance sequences with choreographers Phillip Chbeeb and Makenzie Dustman, with Joya Kazi credited as co-choreographer. Each number was approached with a single guiding question, she says: “What is the essence we are trying to bring out in this particular moment?” Where a typical Bollywood dance sequence gets five days to shoot, the production often had just one. The choreography also draws on multiple regional styles, including Kuthu, Bharatanatyam and Pakistani-influenced dance, reflecting the mix of identities on the fictional team. Priyanka Kedia, Lena Khan and Maitreyi Ramakrishnan on the sets of “Best of the Best” Netflix Khan, whose credits include the independent feature “The Tiger Hunter,” says the industry’s relationship to South Asian stories has shifted since that film came out in 2016, even as some structural limits remain. “We still don’t have that many romances or romantic comedies with South Asians,” she says, pointing out that South Asian men are often not given the chance to play the lead. The film flips that dynamic elsewhere in its own casting, she notes: “The nerdy minority character is actually a white guy. Like we have a token white guy.” She also credits a wave of South Asian musicians and actors, including Joy Crookes, whose song she fought to include in the soundtrack, with making the film possible. “And now we’re like, well, we’ve really made it when we make a movie that’s just good,” she says. That philosophy extended to how much cultural context the film explains for a global Netflix audience. Khan says she resisted pressure to over-explain South Asian references, trusting shows like “Never Have I Ever” to have already proven audiences do not need everything spelled out. “At some point this country and the world is just full of people in different cultures,” she says. Working with Minhaj and Venkataramanujam, both first-time feature writers, meant frequent creative disagreements, Khan says, but never without purpose. “There would be such a thoughtful reason that we were always fighting over why we’re doing a certain thing, but it was never for a vapid reason,” she says. “And they’re also just the most gracious people.” Hasan Minhaj – “Best of the Best” Netflix Looking ahead, Khan says she is drawn to projects centered on overlooked people or subjects, alongside a personal passion project already underway. “I’m always on the hunt for that,” she says, describing a search for stories she wishes already existed and a way to make them for a wide audience. “Best of the Best” also stars Lilly Singh, Nihar Duvvuri, Nico Greetham, Amryn Khurana, Tanishq Joshi, Saara Chaudry and Sasha Bhasin. It is streaming now on Netflix. title: ‘Resident Evil’: What Critics Are Saying About Zach Cregger’s New Horror Film
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 18, 2026 12:09am Austin Abrams in 'Resident Evil.' Dušan Martinček/Sony Pictures Logo text Zach Cregger ‘s Resident Evil has arrived — and the critics are embracing the latest reimaginging on the long-running video game franchise. Based on the popular Capcom video games, Resident Evil stars Austin Abrams as Bryan, an outmatched medical courier who becomes trapped in a monster outbreak in Raccoon City during a single night of chaos and has to try to survive. The Sony Pictures ‘ film reunites Abrams with his Weapons director Cregger, who also co-wrote the script. The cast also features Zach Cherry, Kali Reis and Paul Walter Hauser. Related Stories Movies 'Resident Evil' Racing Toward Healthy Box Office Haul for Zach Cregger's Reboot Movies Zach Cregger on Revamping 'Resident Evil' and Why He Doubts He'll Ever Return to Comedy While Cregger’s take on Resident Evil is the eighth installment in the live-action franchise, it’s also a reboot and serves as a fresh start. Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter earlier this week, Cregger defended his decision to scrap the games’ legacy characters. Responding to online pushback, he said, “I know that when you dive into an IP you’re going to get flack, a certain degree, from the fandom. It would be weird if I were shocked that that was happening. But I think that when the people who love these games the way I do see the movie, my hope is that they feel seen and they feel like this movie is paying homage to the games, because it is, it’s obvious.” As of publication, it has an 96 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes and a 91 percent audience score. As the movie enters theaters , THR has rounded up what critics are saying, below. THR’s Frank Scheck, wrote in his review , “Abrams’ shaggy appeal as the everyman hero who somehow manages to overcome every obstacle thrown in his way, including the most monstrous creatures Cregger and his talented creative team could devise, is a key factor in the film’s success. Filled with baroque gore and wildly imaginative set pieces delivered at a feverish pace, Resident Evil transcends its simplistic premise with the sort of cinematic wit and flair for which the filmmaker has been justly acclaimed.” IGN’s Tom Jorgensen wrote, “Whatever your idea of what a good Resident Evil movie should be, I have to recommend to the skeptical to put that to one side and lock in for what Zach Cregger delivers with this new adaptation of the Capcom games. With a clear appreciation for odds stacked against the protagonist and all manner of freaky foes to stand against them, Cregger ably adapts the spirit, if not the letter, of the Resident Evil games into a jet-fueled horror experience that has room for lots of tension, some great laughs, and a strong central performance from Austin Abrams.” He added, “With a tendency towards celebrating the feel of the games and not the specifics of the plot, Resident Evil succeeds in amplifying classic gameplay moments into horror movie beats in a way that goes far beyond simple fan service.” The New York Times’ Brandon Yu praised the tone, writing, “It’s a thriller that’s as funny as it is jumpy, with a remarkable number of jokes rooted simply in Abrams either shrieking in fear or muttering with incredulity. Cregger weaponizes comedy not only as an irrepressible reflex, but as a tool: If horror is about tension and release, he sees the relief of a laugh the same way he might a scream. But it only works because of Abrams. The movie is essentially a one-man show.” Meanwhile, YouTube critic Jeremy Jahns said the humor “they could have pulled it back a little bit to make the last act a little smoother.” Overall, however, he added, “I actually really enjoyed it. The nods were there without feeling like nostalgia bait. The vibe, the fish out of water scenario that grows bigger and bigger as the film goes on does decidedly feel like Resident Evil. Also, it is decidedly and works well as a Zach Cregger horror film. I guess these two concepts just work well together. And I thought Austin Abrams did a great job carrying us through it. This movie being a Resident Evil dark horror comedy was a surprise to be sure, but a welcome one.” Inverse’s Chrishaun Baker explained that the movie, “playfully engages with the first, is totally uninterested in the second, and cashes all in on the third. For a movie and a filmmaker to have spent months at ground zero of a battle over what form video game adaptations should take, it’s ironic that Resident Evil would end up being one of the best video game films ever made. By bucking the cloying attempts at “pleasing fans” that have sunk so many other movies of this kind, Zach Cregger has made the platonic ideal of what a video game movie should be: a cinematic experience that approximates the medium-specific idiosyncrasies of the game, while offering something new and satisfying for fans and newcomers.” The Guardians’s Jesse Hassenger compared it to Cregger’s prior film, writing, “ Weapons had a creepy, evocative aversion to simple metaphorical reads that ultimately increased its effectiveness; the same isn’t quite true here. Resident Evil foregrounds one obvious bit of character change for Bryan, but after doing a great job making us care about him for more than 90 minutes, Cregger seems to abandon him a few steps shy of completing any real journey. Is he awaiting a level up that never arrives? Hard to say. But maybe bringing a video game sensibility to the big screen while keeping any gamer cheesiness on the margins is journey enough.” THR

title: Alfonso Cuaron to Make First Korea Visit at Busan as Festival Also Spotlights European Women+ Filmmakers
full_text: Sep 17, 2026 11:43pm PT Alfonso Cuaron to Make First Korea Visit at Busan as Festival Also Spotlights European Women+ Filmmakers By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Japan’s Top Broadcasters Unite for First Joint Delegation to MipCancun (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ 2 hours ago ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ 4 hours ago See All Michelle Quance The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has announced the first-ever Korea visit by Alfonso Cuarón, alongside a dedicated spotlight on nine films from European women and genderqueer filmmakers. Cuarón, who has won the Academy Award for best director twice, for “Gravity” (2013) and “Roma” (2018), also holds the Venice Film Festival’s best screenplay prize for “Y Tu Mamá También” (2001) and a Golden Lion for “Roma.” He first caught Hollywood’s attention with “Y Tu Mamá También,” a portrait of youth and desire, before taking “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban” (2004) in a moodier, more personal visual direction than the series had gone before, and later used extended long takes in “Children of Men” (2007) to pull audiences directly into a world at war. He is expected to appear at BIFF’s opening ceremony and will sit down for an extended conversation with festivalgoers about the camera language and instincts behind his films. An Imax screening of “Gravity,” co-written with his son, filmmaker Jonás Cuarón, will also be at the festival. Related Stories ‘On Behalf of My Son’ Director Gabriel Martins on Black Brazilian Representation in His Films: ‘It’s a Life Project To Me, Not Just Cinema’ BBC, Bobby Prod, Folivari, Gao Shan Pictures Honored by Europe's Animation Industry at Cartoon Forum Jonás Cuarón’s latest feature, “Campeón Gabacho,” will have its Asian premiere in the World Cinema section, followed by a post-screening Q&A. Since writing on “Gravity,” the younger Cuarón has built his own filmography with “Desierto” (2015) and “Chupa” (2023). “Campeón Gabacho,” starring Juan Daniel García Treviño, Leslie Grace, Rubén Blades, Eddie Marsan, Rosario Dawson and Cheech Marin, follows a Mexican immigrant building a life in the United States, and was produced by Jonás Cuarón alongside his father and Gabriela Rodriguez under their Esperanto Filmoj banner, with Nicolás Celis also producing. Popular on Variety Elsewhere at the festival, BIFF is showcasing “Europe! Voices of Women+ in Film,” a program run with the European Film Promotion (EFP), spotlighting nine officially selected films through targeted promotion and industry networking. The lineup spans period drama, documentary and contemporary narrative work built around questions of freedom, memory and family, with four of the nine as feature debuts. May el-Toukhy ‘s “Woman Unknown,” winner of the Golden Lion at Venice, anchors the group; el-Toukhy became the first Danish woman filmmaker to take that prize, while Mathilde Arcel won the Volpi Cup for best actress in the same film. Also included are Marine Atlan’s debut “La Gradiva,” Pegah Ahangarani’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime,” winner of the Un Certain Regard Prize at Cannes, Margherita Ferrari’s debut “Föa – Once Upon a Future,” Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,” Marie Kreutzer’s “Gentle Monster,” Shahrbanoo Sadat’s “No Good Men” and Sarah Arnold’s debut “Too Many Beasts.” Judith Godrèche’s “A Girl’s Story,” part of this year’s gala presentations, joins Angela Schanelec’s “My Wife Cries,” Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak’s “Birds of War,” Jacqueline Lentzou’s “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” winner of the Horizons Award for Best Director at Venice, and Konstantina Kotzamani’s “Titanic Ocean” among the additional selections. Five directors from the program, el-Toukhy, Godrèche, Ferrari, Lentzou and Kotzamani, will travel to Busan to present their films. Godrèche will also take part in a Cine Class session, “Women, Rewriting the Screen,” and BIFF and EFP will co-host a Talk-to-Talk panel, “Women Directors: Taking the Scene,” bringing together Ferrari, el-Toukhy and Lentzou alongside Iranian director Marjan Khosravi (“Dreams of the Wild Oaks”), Chinese director Michelle Zhou (“Big Little Things”) and Afghan director Zainab Entezar (“771 Days”). BIFF programmer Seo Seunghee said that in reviewing films for this year’s festival, she noticed European women directors becoming more prominent among the strongest titles under consideration, in both volume and quality. “Moreover, the fact that four of the nine invited films are feature debuts is also an indicator of the generational shift taking place in European cinema,” Seo said. “Our ongoing collaboration with EFP has become a reliable channel for discovering and validating outstanding films and filmmakers, and the results are fully reflected in this year’s lineup.” EFP managing director Irina Ignatiew-Lemke said the “Europe! Voices of Women+ in Film” initiative lets EFP and its member organizations “join forces to give distinctive European voices greater international visibility.” She added, “Busan is an important platform for bringing these filmmakers and their works into dialogue with audiences and industry professionals in Asia. By combining the festival’s selection with EFP’s targeted promotion and networking, we are proud to support underrepresented voices and create opportunities for the next generation of women+ filmmakers.” The program runs in collaboration with BIFF, the Sydney Film Festival and Festival do Rio, with support from the Creative Europe – MEDIA Programme of the European Union. This year’s participating national film promotion organizations are Austrian Films, Cinecittà, the Czech Film Center, the Danish Film Institute, German Films and Unifrance, with Cineuropa serving as media partner. The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and venues throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13. title: ‘Tenzing’ Actor Tenzin Dalha Unveiled as Male Lead in Bengali Thriller ‘Chheledhora’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 17, 2026 11:08pm PT ‘Tenzing’ Actor Tenzin Dalha Unveiled as Male Lead in Bengali Thriller ‘Chheledhora’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ 3 hours ago ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ 5 hours ago Alfonso Cuaron to Make First Korea Visit at Busan as Festival Also Spotlights European Women+ Filmmakers 7 hours ago See All Getty Images Tenzin Dalha , at the Toronto Film Festival with Jennifer Peedom’s Apple original Film “ Tenzing ,” has been revealed as the male lead in Bengali-language thriller “ Chheledhora ,” opposite Swastika Mukherjee. His casting had been withheld when the Indo-American production was first announced earlier this year, with producers naming only Mukherjee at that point. “Tenzing,” a gala presentation at TIFF, features Genden Phuntsok as legendary mountaineer Tenzing Norgay, with Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe and Caitríona Balfe also in the cast. A limited theatrical run begins Oct. 9, with global streaming on Apple TV following Oct. 16. Popular on Variety Related Stories MoreThan Films Acquires Serville Poblete’s Buzzy Toronto Hangout Comedy ‘Sunburn’ (EXCLUSIVE) 'I Play Rocky,' 'Elsinore' and 'Tangles' Signal an Oscar Season About the Craft of Acting and Memory In “Chheledhora,” written and directed by Shieladitya Moulik – whose credits include “Sweater” and “Surjo” – Dalha and Mukherjee anchor a story set off by an act of parental defiance. Mukherjee plays Brishti, a divorced mother who “steals” her own daughter for a birthday outing, only for the child to be genuinely abducted. The discovery then draws a group of deeply flawed adults and their children into an erratic journey through Northeast India, where the youngest characters gradually emerge as the moral compass for the adults around them. Filmed extensively in Arunachal Pradesh’s Ziro Valley, the production combines family drama, thriller elements and dark humor with the cultural texture of India’s Northeast. It is currently in post-production. “We made a very conscious decision not to announce Tenzin when we first revealed ‘Chheledhora,'” said Ann Mukherjee, founder of Indo-American production company Sita22 Films. “We knew he had this extraordinary international moment ahead of him with ‘Tenzing,’ and TIFF felt like exactly the right time for audiences to discover another side of him. Tenzin possesses a quiet emotional intelligence and restraint that makes him a fascinating counterpoint to Swastika’s tremendous emotional force. Their chemistry is central to the film.” Mukherjee described “Chheledhora” as a film that makes both a physical and emotional journey into India’s Northeast. “We want to tell stories that are deeply rooted in India but aren’t constrained by conventional ideas of language, geography or identity,” she said. Dalha said it felt “particularly special” to be discussing one project while at the festival for another. “They are completely different films, yet rooted in human grit, empathy, the lengths to which humans are capable of going for people they love,” he said. “What drew me to ‘Chheledhora’ was Shieladitya’s writing. His understanding of humans as imperfect complex beings and looking at life beyond the dichotomy of individuals as good or bad. He wrote these beautiful broken young adult characters making questionable choices for their loved ones.” The actor described Mukherjee as “a force of nature in frame and a force of joy on set,” adding that the Arunachal landscape shaped the film’s atmosphere from the outset. “Shooting in Ziro and Arunachal Pradesh provided the perfect backdrop for a thriller, and the weather set the tone right for the ambience,” he said. The film is produced by Ann Mukherjee for Sita22 Films, with Jitin Hingorani as co-producer and creative producer, Dhanraj Sawant as executive producer and Priyangi Borthakur as supervising producer. Italian cinematographer Vincenzo Condorelli shot the film. “The idea was never to make a Bengali film that simply happens to travel to the Northeast,” said Hingorani, who also heads content and development at Sita22 Films. “The journey changes these characters, and the Northeast becomes part of the film’s emotional language. Pairing Swastika and Tenzin gives us two performers coming from very different cinematic and cultural energies, and that tension is part of what makes the film so exciting. title: ‘Resident Evil’ Scaring Up Franchise Best Previews With $8M-$9M & Rotten Tomatoes 91% Audience Score
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony Curry Barker, Alex Gibney, Siân Heder, Rachel Morrison & Bassam Tariq On Taking Chances & Conquering Obstacles – Deadline & DGA’s Art Of Directing At TIFF ‘Dark Winds’ Zahn McClarnon Receiving Santa Fe International Film Festival’s Visionary Award ‘Obsession’ Star Megan Lawless Boards Indie Romantic Comedy ‘Crushed’ View All September 17, 2026 10:28pm Austin Abrams in 'Resident Evil' Sony Buckle up your 4DX seat because it’s gonna be a fun weekend as out of the gate, Zach Cregger ‘s take on Resident Evil is already posting the best previews ever for the franchise with tonight north of $8M and maybe even north of $9M . The outlook going into the weekend was $40M-$50M. Those who are smart, inside the industry and study ticket sales believe the movie has a shot to go over $50M. Similar to how this Resident Evil is posting the series best critical score on Rotten Tomatoes (now at 96% certified fresh), so is it posting the best audience score as well at 91%. On Rotten Tomatoes, the previous best audience score belonged to the original 2002 film at 67%. Related Stories News Audiences Flocking To Anime On Netflix At 10 Times The Rate Of Other Genres, Report Reveals News 'Resident Evil' To Scorch The Earth With $80M Global Debut - Box Office Preview Previews for the Sony /Constantin R-rated feature adaptation of the Capcom video game began at 2PM stateside. Watch on Deadline Tonight’s estimated take easily decimates the franchise’s previous high (which wasn’t much), 2016’s Resident Evil: Final Chapter at $1M. That was the first time a Resident Evil movie posted seven digits in its previews. But get a load of this: Resident Evil ‘s previews even on the low-end of $8M scorch Cregger’s Weapons ($5.75M previews, $43.5M opening), Scream 7 (yes, $7.8M, $63.6M opening, but put a pin in that one), Mortal Kombat 2 ($5.2M, $38.5M, a Midway video game adapted into an R-rated franchise), Sonic the Hedgehog 3 ($6.5M, $60.1M; yes, we know that’s a family film, but it’s based on a video game. Calm down). Here’s the thing, the Friday/preview-to-Saturday holds for some previous Resident Evil movies are pretty good with The Final Chapter +1.4% between those two days, the original 2002 movie +1%, and Resident Evil: Afterlife -9%, that pic holding the series previous domestic opening record at $26.6M). The point is, because it’s horror, and because it’s a different iteration of Resident Evil from the previous Milla Jovovich films, the wait-and-see is just how front loaded this movie is. Scream 7 was a completely different animal in the return of Neve Campbell to the franchise and tracking sources tonight advise not to comp Resident Evil to that horror pic (at least not yet). It was Cregger’s vision here to make a more authentic adaptation of the games which he has avidly played. The net $75M Constantin/Sony production of Resident Evil is playing in PLFs and Imax, with the latter format’s 70MM still on a crusade with The Odyssey (about 35 auditoriums). Tonight’s figures come from distribution sources, not the studio, so take everything with a grain of salt.
