title: Macklemore Alleged to Have Repeated Palestine Comments Despite Promoter Assurances to NFL Stadium Owners (Report)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 10:18pm From left: Ed Sheeran, Robert Kraft and Macklemore. Paras Griffin/Getty Images for for iHeartRadio; Aaron J. Thornton/WireImage; Allen Berezovsky/Getty Images The Macklemore controversy rumbles on, with new reporting alleging that assurances were given to a group of NFL stadium owners that the rapper would not repeat any comments on the issue of Palestine during Macklemore’s second, and ultimately final, stint as the opening act on Ed Sheeran ‘s tour. In a story published in The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday , the newspaper revealed more details of alleged communication between Sheeran, the promoters of Sheeran’s Loop Tour and NFL stadium owners, including New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft , after concerns were raised over Macklemore declaring “Free Palestine” on stage before performing “Hind’s Hall”, his pro-Palestinian song at the MetLife Stadium concert on Sept. 4. Related Stories Music Robert Kraft Responds After Macklemore Invites Him to Match His $1M Donation to Support Palestinian People Music Ed Sheeran Openers Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe Depart Tour in Solidarity With Macklemore After the incident, the WSJ reports that representatives of Kraft and other NFL stadium owners — including Carolina Panthers owner David Tepper, Atlanta Falcons owner Arthur Blank and Philadelphia Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie — reached out to Loop Tour promoters Messina Touring Group about Macklemore’s overtly political comments. The owners were alleged to have been told that Macklemore, who was initially set to feature on 10 dates for Sheeran, would not bring up the issue of Palestine again during his performances. At the Sept. 5 concert at the MetLife Stadium, however, the Grammy-winning artist said: “One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine! I want to say this to all of my Jewish brothers and sisters. Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you.” Macklemore’s comments on the second of the two Metlife Stadium concerts were picked up by news outlets after the Israeli-American Council petitioned for Sheeran to remove the rapper from his tour. Other pressure groups such as StopAntisemitism and Combat Antisemitism Movement as well as the singer Pink also called for the rapper’s removal. The WSJ reports that behind the scenes, Kraft and Sheeran had a 40-minute phone call about the Macklemore controversy. Kraft is claimed to have told Sheeran that while he had sympathy for the Palestinian people, Macklemore’s comments in his estimation constituted hate speech, and was not a free speech issue. After days of media scrutiny and with concerns about the future viability of the Loop Tour without access to NFL stadiums, Messina released a statement on Sept. 14 that Macklemore was dropped from the remaining eight U.S. tour dates. In a statement to Rolling Stone , Messina said: “As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming U.S. tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans. After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.” After being dropped, Macklemore released a lengthy statement about the controversy . “Before I get into it, I want to say something that should be obvious. In this moment I think it matters. I am not a victim,” Macklemore wrote on Instagram. “Ed Sheeran is not a victim. Pink is not a victim. We have careers, money, opportunities, safety and audiences around the world. Whatever consequences any of us face for what we say, we get to go home to our families. The victims are the Palestinian people.” Sheeran also released a lengthy statement after Macklemore’s removal . “After Macklemore’s performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting. I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said. I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge. One of those people was Robert Kraft. I was also involved in direct talks with promoters along with activists on both sides to try and find a mutual resolution for all, but the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final.“ Sheeran then reiterated, “Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine. Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.” Macklemore’s removal set off a fire storm, with Sheeran’s other support acts Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and his backing band Beoga all pulling out of the remaining tour dates in solidarity with the “Thrift Store” rapper. On Sept. 16, Macklemore announced that he would donate his earnings from the Loop Tour, approximately $1 million , to six organizations supporting Palestinians and called on Kraft to match his donation. Kraft responded by donating $2 million. THR

title: ‘Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story’ Review: Ryan Murphy’s Latest Netflix Serial Killer Saga Is Faux-Feminist Nonsense
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 9:30pm 'Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story' In the final hour of Netflix’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story , the titular murderess, having finally made her peace with the act of violence that has defined her life, turns to the loyal companion who’s been by her side through it all. “Okay,” she says. “Let’s make it mean something.” Lizzie (Ella Beatty) is talking about her wealth and notoriety, which she wishes to channel into a force for good. In the moment, though, all I could hear was showrunner Ian Brennan muttering that sentiment to himself. The latest addition to his and Ryan Murphy ’s murder-verse tries desperately to draw something, anything meaningful out of Borden’s saga, with all the finesse of a college freshman trying to crank out a 15-page term paper in the two hours before deadline — and with all the same power of persuasion. Related Stories TV Homer Gere Shares His Theory About 'The Shards' and Robert Mallory TV 'Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story' Team on Painting a Portrait of Female Rage -- and Leaning into Lesbian Theories Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story The Bottom Line Lots of killers, tons of filler. Airdate: Thursday, Sept. 17 (Netflix) Cast: Ella Beatty, Vicky Krieps, Charlie Hunnam, Rebecca Hall, Sarah Paulson, Jessica Barden, Joey Pollari, Billie Lourd Creators: Ryan Murphy, Ian Brennan As the subtitle indicates, Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is first and foremost a retelling of the real events you probably first heard of as a playground chant (one whose melody becomes a recurring motif), or perhaps saw depicted in more detail by Chloë Sevigny and Kristen Stewart in 2018’s Lizzie . While the real-life Borden has always denied responsibility for the August 1892 deaths of her father and stepmother, the series wastes no time playing coy; it takes as settled fact that it was indeed Lizzie who wielded the axe. As for why , there, too, the series has a clear-cut answer: because they’re emotional sadists whose sole pleasures in life are tormenting the help and insulting their daughter. Playing Abby and Andrew, Rebecca Hall and Charlie Hunnam gorge on the scenery like they’re trying to make themselves sick; one dinner sequence even ends with them spewing geysers of vomit. There’s zero nuance to their performances, and also nothing unique about them to make them memorable. But as a way to get you to sympathize with the devilish Ms. Borden, I can’t say their cartoonish villainy is ineffective. The only real question left is the how , and that too is more or less established in the Max Winkler-directed premiere. Vicky Krieps plays Maggie, a new housemaid who makes an immediate impression on the family with her skill, her work ethic and her anachronistic style (punk shags in Manic Panic shades, literally a century before they’ll be cool). Lizzie falls in love practically at first sight, and Maggie seems charmed right back. Under Maggie’s guidance, the sweet, shy, sheltered girl who’d never so much as heard of la petite mort blossoms into one confident enough to start rattling the gilded cage her parents have trapped her in. At Maggie’s suggestion, she begins to wonder if killing them might not be her only way out. Then, having put together so many puzzle pieces so quickly, The Lizzie Borden Story finds itself with the problem of having eight hours’ worth of content to fill. I wish I could say that the series has an easy solution for that, too. Instead, it flails about for a number of stalling tactics, none of them particularly satisfying. One is simply to slow down the pace of the storytelling. Bits of exposition are repeated in rapid succession (“It’s the culmination of my life’s ambitions, really,” says a character of a completed project, and then, a few minutes later, “It’s everything I ever dreamed of, really,” just in case you weren’t paying attention the first time). Lizzie and Maggie indulge in dreamy nature idylls that clumsily evoke historical lesbian dramas like Portrait of a Lady on Fire or Ammonite , only, for some reason, with way less sex. Intriguing tangents are brought up to go nowhere — no sooner has the show finally started to explain why Abby sucks so much than it’s done her off, thus nipping in the bud any interest we might have taken in her. The other method, more successful at padding that run time but even more annoying in its spirit, is to insist that The Lizzie Borden Story is actually about something much, much bigger than itself. That Borden is in fact part of a whole historical lineage of female killers, all of whose tales are linked together by some lazily nebulous concept of What It Means to Be a Woman in Society, and that there’s therefore something pretty Female Empowering about the fact that Lizzie has decided to axe-murder her parents, if you really think about it. The show attempts to do all this by braiding Lizzie’s story with those of arguably the only other female killers as famous as she is. In the late 19th century, Lizzie and Maggie spend long hours reading each other the story of Elizabetta Báthory, the 16th-century countess accused of bathing in the blood of virgins. Krieps plays Elizabetta in flashbacks, which adds nothing significant to our understanding of either Elizabetta or Maggie but does provide the actor an opportunity to don another anachronistic hairstyle (this time, it’s severe bangs and tomato-red streaks). Meanwhile, in the 20th century, Lizzie has in turn captivated Aileen Wuornos (played by Sarah Paulson in a broad performance more suited for Saturday Night Live ). The series lavishes much more attention on Aileen than it did Elizabetta — like, to the point where one wonders if what Murphy and Brennan truly wanted was to do Monster: The Aileen Wuornos Story , and were only stopped by the existence of 2003’s Monster , the Aileen Wuornos story. In this Monster ’s telling, Aileen worships Lizzie to the point of booking an overnight stay at her old home and hallucinating interactions with her. To this sex worker turned killer of johns, Lizzie is a role model, a spiritual sister, someone who just gets how the pressures of womanhood can drive a gal to violence. Never mind that none of these three killers have anything in common — not their backgrounds, not their motives, not their methods, not their outcomes. Never mind that The Lizzie Borden Story ’s further attempt to reframe Lizzie as not just a self-actualized independent lady but an outright icon of the women’s suffrage movement comes out of nowhere. Or that for a show supposedly so in tune with the struggles of womanhood, it has no sympathy to extend an embittered wife and mother like Abby (who, for all her abuses, was not a literal murderer ), and no curiosity to offer a rebel like Maggie (whose goals or desires or even personality traits always seem to be changing at the whims of the plot). All of these people, you see, are female. For Monster , that’s reason enough to lump them together — even if, in the end, it has nothing more substantial to say than, “Women be choppin’.” THR

title: ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Review: Shun Oguri and Lily James in a Meandering Franchise Entry From Takashi Miike That’s Semi-Coherent at Best
full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 9:05pm Shun Oguri (center) in 'Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo.' Courtesy of NEON The first in a planned series of international sequels, Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo gets things off to a mostly inauspicious start, despite enlisting the magnetic Shun Oguri as the latest incarnation of the seedy, morally hollow detective to whom the films owe their title. It’s closer in terms of plot machinations to Abel Ferrara’s 1992 original with Harvey Keitel than to Werner Herzog’s wildly eccentric 2009 follow-up, Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans , a snug fit for Nicolas Cage’s gonzo extremes. But that doesn’t mean the choppy narrative ever gathers much steam. What’s surprising is that prolific Japanese cult director Takashi Miike , known for explosions of operatic violence, gore and perversion in breakthrough films like Auditon and Ichi the Killer , delivers a franchise entry that aspires to be a hardboiled crime thriller but lacks the electricity to build suspense or even tension. While devout Miike-heads might feel sated by the one or two amped-up set pieces and the characteristic strain of dark humor, this is by far the weakest of the three Bad Lieutenant s. Related Stories Movies 'The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd' Review: Amanda Seyfried and Scoot McNairy Bring Raw Intensity to Tim Blake Nelson's Death Row Drama Movies 'Re/Pair' Review: David Schwimmer, W. Kamau Bell and Van Jones Lead Pragmatic Doc About the Past and Present of Black-Jewish Relations Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo The Bottom Line A sluggish neo-noir oddly lacking in tension. Venue : Toronto International Film Festival (Special Presentations) Cast : Shun Oguri, Lily James, Shotaro Mamiya, Liv Morgan, Jun Kunimura, Hiroshi Tachi, Shuhei Nomura, Nanase Nishino, Yuka Kouri Director : Takashi Miike Screenwriter : Daisuke Tengan Rated R, 1 hour 48 minutes The characters played by Keitel and Cage in previous installments both experienced a drug-fueled spiritual crisis. A cynical cop with a long history of investigating the yakuza underworld, Yabuki (Oguri) doesn’t appear to have much on his mind beyond feeding his meth habit, playing ping pong and doing drugs with a couple of giggly Korean sex-workers, and keeping the loan sharks at bay as he attempts to pay off — or recklessly increase — his gambling debts. He is occasionally troubled by guilt over his role in the death of a partner 15 years earlier, but those thoughts surface in surreal dream states rather than serious self-reflection. Yabuki’s marriage is already in such a shambles that even his preteen kids are losing their faith in him. He scarcely blinks when he comes home and finds a note from his wife saying she has left with the children and telling him not to try to find them. With the yakuza syndicates in a transitional state as old clans dissolve and new ones are formed deeper underground, his colleagues in law enforcement call on Yabuki’s expertise when a naked body turns up, an extensively tattooed young gangster whose neck has been neatly snapped. Yabuki recognizes the victim but withholds that information from the cops, instead using it to chip away at his debts. While that investigation is ongoing, another spate of murders comes to light as Ishizuka (Shotaro Mamiya), a disenfranchised yakuza soldier fresh out of prison, wanders around town with a hefty machete delivering payback to anyone who betrayed him. He starts with his wife, chopping her up and then rolling her remains into meatballs, served up in planter boxes on the terrace for crows to feast on — inarguably the movie’s most quintessentially macabre Miike touch. More criminal than cop in the eyes of many, including himself, Yabuki is an outsider at the precinct. But he hangs around long enough to be roped into assisting American FBI agent Gwen Birgssen ( Lily James ) in an investigation. Gwen has been dispatched to Tokyo to track down Megan (current Women’s World Champion WWE wrestler Liv Morgan), the missing daughter of a prominent U.S. congressman who came to Japan to study the art of sushi and got sidetracked by drugs and thugs. It later emerges that in addition to crack and raw bar cuisine, Megan has a thing for short dudes with impressive body ink. It’s this thread more than anything that derails any plot momentum, partly because James is so woefully miscast, assuming an unconvincing Southern Fried drawl you might expect to find in a regional theater staging of Tennessee Williams. The Brit actress has obviously put in time on the fight training, demonstrating nimble moves in a nightclub brawl with no bearing on the plot. It does serve, however, to get both Gwen and Yabuki so sexually charged that they tumble into bed together. The old fight-and-f*ck combo never fails. Miike appears to have minimal interest in dialogue-driven scenes. That’s too bad because Gwen and Yabuki have a few of them in which key information is possibly shared. Between James’ garbled twang, Oguri’s unsteady command of English (the actor fared better in that regard in Godzilla vs. Kong ) and a muddy sound mix, much of their conversation is incomprehensible. Which might be for the best considering the increasingly bonkers twists of the script by Daisuke Tengan, who collaborated with Miike on Audition and the hit samurai epic, 13 Assassins . The two investigations do eventually intersect of course, which happens when another slender tatted-up young gangster turns up dead and the victim’s father (Jun Kunimura, immortalized as Boss Tanaka in Kill Bill: Vol. 1 ) cuts Yabuki a deal to clear all his debts with the Chinese mob if the cop delivers the killer to him. The inevitable bloodbath happens, along with lots more meatballs for the hungry crows and revelations about how Megan gets her freak on. But the cases are resolved too haphazardly to make us care much, especially when it involves Gwen, the least persuasive gunslinger in the history of movies, snarling “Motherfucker” as she plugs a mobster full of lead. Like much of Miike’s work, the visuals are equal parts slick and rough-edged, and the Shinjuku setting, specifically the red-light Kabukicho district with its warren of back alleys, bars and brothels, supplies plenty of shadowy atmosphere, often stained with neon. But the movie is way too busy to keep all its plates spinning and if not for the fact that Oguri is so watchable with his mop of unruly hair and sleepy deadpan delivery, there would be very little here to recommend. But Miike fans might even give Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo a stamp of approval just for one scene of major mayhem, in which Yabuki does some virtuoso driving, plowing through yakuza scum while protecting the lives of … a bunch of cute kids? Don’t even ask. title: Barbra Streisand Slams Trump’s “Unchecked Ego” Amid His Kennedy Center Demolition Threats
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All September 17, 2026 7:35pm Barbra Streisand onstage at the 2026 Oscars. Kevin Winter/Getty Images Barbra Streisand is criticizing President Donald Trump over his controversial handling of the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. The EGOT winner released a statement on her official website Thursday, a day after an image that photojournalists captured through the windows of Air Force One showed Trump examining a poster board that appeared to display the words: “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.” “In 2008, I was deeply honored to be included in the 31st annual class of Kennedy Center Honorees. For me, and for so many artists, that honor represented something larger than a career recognition. It represented a belief in the importance of art to the life of a democracy,” Streisand wrote. “That is why what is happening to the Kennedy Center is so galling and painful to witness.” Related Stories Business Jon Voight Explains What He's Up to as Trump's Special Ambassador to Hollywood News Kennedy Center's Abrupt Plan to Shut Down May Spark Further Legal Battles Her comments came as a district judge in Washington instructed the Kennedy Center on Thursday to provide at least 30 days’ notice before carrying out any significant changes to their renovation or construction plan, “including but not limited to any ‘demolition’ of the center’s main building,” The New York Times reported . The Kennedy Center has been at the center of a legal battle as Trump has slammed a court decision to block his name, two times now, from being added to the building’s exterior. On Wednesday, the president told reporters that the arts institution may be “ripped down” if his name does not appear on the building, CNN reported . Streisand continued, “When Donald Trump attempted to put his name alongside the late President Kennedy’s on the building’s entrance, the move was met with widespread opposition from artists and much of the public. A federal judge subsequently ruled that the Kennedy Center’s name could not be changed without an act of Congress, and Trump’s name was removed from the building’s façade. “Yet the fight continued. After his name was removed, a humiliated Trump ordered a large tarp placed over the façade, where it remains today. The Trump-aligned board then relentlessly lobbied again to add his name, prompting another federal ruling that blocked their effort,” she said. “And now, a thoroughly defeated Trump has announced that the Kennedy Center is being closed for what the completely stacked board describes as a major renovation. Oddly, when Trump’s name was still on the building, there was no discussion of closing it! “You can easily imagine my indignation at seeing this revered institution become the subject of such a bitter struggle over one man’s name and unchecked ego,” Streisand added in her statement, which also included a photo of her and John F. Kennedy in 1963, as well as an image of her and Morgan Freeman at the 31st annual Kennedy Center Honors in 2008. Read Streisand’s full statement below. In 1964, in the aftermath of President John F. Kennedy’s shocking assassination, Congress passed legislation designating the National Cultural Center as a living memorial to him. The Kennedy family and other American leaders wanted a meaningful way to preserve his legacy. Re-naming the Cultural Center in JFK’s honor was a fitting choice, because he was a true champion of the arts. Since then, the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts has stood as one of America’s great cultural venues. Many of the world’s most accomplished actors, musicians, singers and dancers have graced its stages. In 2008, I was deeply honored to be included in the 31st annual class of Kennedy Center Honorees. For me, and for so many artists, that honor represented something larger than a career recognition. It represented a belief in the importance of art to the life of a democracy. That is why what is happening to the Kennedy Center is so galling and painful to witness. When Donald Trump attempted to put his name alongside the late President Kennedy’s on the building’s entrance, the move was met with widespread opposition from artists and much of the public. A federal judge subsequently ruled that the Kennedy Center’s name could not be changed without an act of Congress, and Trump’s name was removed from the building’s façade. Yet the fight continued. After his name was removed, a humiliated Trump ordered a large tarp placed over the façade, where it remains today. The Trump-aligned board then relentlessly lobbied again to add his name, prompting another federal ruling that blocked their effort. And now, a thoroughly defeated Trump has announced that the Kennedy Center is being closed for what the completely stacked board describes as a major renovation. Oddly, when Trump’s name was still on the building, there was no discussion of closing it! You can easily imagine my indignation at seeing this revered institution become the subject of such a bitter struggle over one man’s name and unchecked ego. It is difficult not to think about what President Kennedy himself would have envisioned for the Center: not a monument frozen in time, but a living place where artists could challenge, inspire, provoke, and bring Americans together through the transformative power of the arts. The Kennedy Center was meant to pay tribute to a beloved president, and to advance his philosophy that artistic achievement was proof of a free society. He believed that when the creative impulse cannot flourish freely, a society loses its vitality. Yet another reason why it is so important that Americans exercise their right to vote in the upcoming midterm elections! THR

title: ‘Vintage Violence’ Review: Eugene Kotlyarenko’s Blood-Splattered Rom-Com Is A Fun Crime-Fueled Trip Through Japan’s Denim Trade — Toronto Film Festival
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Hudson Williams Teases ‘Heated Rivalry’ Season 2, Worrying He’s “Doing An Impression” Of Shane: “It Was Surreal” Greta Gerwig On Why She Chose Meryl Streep To Voice Aslan In ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’ View All September 17, 2026 6:40pm Kiko Mizuhara and Cole Sprouse in 'Vintage Violence' WME Six years after his unhinged social media age horror Spree , writer/director Eugene Kotlyarenko takes a more optimistic approach with his action-packed rom-com out of Japan. In Vintage Violence , Carter ( Cole Sprouse ) is an urban explorer who finds a haul of rare denim in a mineshaft. When Izumi ( Kiko Mizuhara ) invites him to offload the merchandise in Tokyo, the pair ends up in the crosshairs of the yakuza in a twisty, high-octane trip through the country’s thriving denim market. Much how he used the found footage of a livestream in Spree to contribute to the social media atmosphere, Kotlyarenko similarly introduces this world with Carter’s urbex stream in Colorado, which Izumi watches on the other side of the world in Toyko. It’s an interesting use of modern tech to drive the narrative, painting a quick but thorough portrait of these two strangers before they even meet. Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline's Reviews Festivals Curry Barker, Alex Gibney, Siân Heder, Rachel Morrison & Bassam Tariq On Taking Chances & Conquering Obstacles - Deadline & DGA's Art Of Directing At TIFF Kotlyarenko also cleverly uses the connectivity of an abandoned AirPod to provide an adrenaline-fueling soundtrack for an intense chase scene, which makes utilizes the skipping music to build the chaotic tension. Watch on Deadline Being as Vintage Violence explores the potential of human connection via the internet, sharing locations becomes the ultimate sign of trust and intimacy in this perpetually online rom-com. Sprouse and Mizuhara manage to establish a believable chemistry as they flirtatiously get to know each other in the virtual opening montage, bringing a playful infatuated quality to their dynamic before they’re even in the same room. While act one gets us invested in their budding romance, all hell breaks loose in act two with an entertaining ensemble of bad guys on their trail. Nijirô Murakami slips effortlessly into the role of Izumi’s shady boyfriend Hiro, who masterminds a shady plot involving Carter’s denim after he racks up debt with the yakuza. Hio Miyazawa channels his inner eccentric Bond villain as Edoga, a dangerous denim-obsessed yakuza boss. But it’s Pierre Taki as the disgraced gangster Ko who gives a devilishly fun performance, seeking vengeance years after his finger was taken as punishment. Using Tokyo as the film’s setting provides gritty, vibrant playground for Kotlyarenko to explore a twisty yakuza plot and shed light on Japan’s growing sex tourism industry, which has come to attracts unsavory visitors from the US. Meanwhile, the film uses the symbolism of denim to represent the old glory of America as a beacon of the West. Don’t let the title fool you. If Spree was Kotlyarenko’s cynical comedic take on horror in the social media age, Vintage Violence is an optimistic rom-com with an exciting action twist, that’s still not afraid of a little gross-out factor—not just in the form of the quintessential Japanese blood spray, but also a graphically detailed makeout scene that will have audiences losing it. Vintage Violence is an addictive fusion of genre set through Kotlyarenko’s hyper-stylized cinematic aesthetic, which is grounded seamlessly by charming performances from Sprouse and Mizuhara. title: ‘Resident Evil’ Racing Toward Healthy Box Office Haul for Zach Cregger’s Reboot
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All September 17, 2026 6:38pm Austin Abrams in 'Resident Evil.' Courtesy of Everett Collection Logo text Resident Evil looks to get off to a running start in its opening weekend at the box office . Sony Pictures releases writer-director Zach Cregger ‘s horror-survival video game adaptation on Friday in roughly 3,500 North American theaters, with the studio projecting a debut frame of $40 million for the three-day weekend. This is in line with third-party tracking services, although some of those have upped their expectations in recent days as interest heats up, with the possibility that the opening gets close to $50 million or higher. It carries a $75 million production budget. Related Stories Movies Zach Cregger on Revamping 'Resident Evil' and Why He Doubts He'll Ever Return to Comedy Movies 'Resident Evil' Review: Zach Cregger Gives a Fatigued Franchise an Exhilarating Shot in the Arm A launch of $40 million would give the new Resident Evil the distinction of the highest-grossing opening in the history of the franchise. The series’ previous titles have collectively grossed more than $1.2 billion worldwide. Hailing from TriStar Pictures, Constantin Film and Davis Film, Resident Evil stars Austin Abrams , Zach Cherry, Kali Reis and Paul Walter Hauser in the story of a medical courier (Abrams) attempting to deliver a precious item in the midst of a deadly viral outbreak in Raccoon City. The movie looks to continue the hot streak for Cregger, whose most recent release was Warner Bros.’ Oscar-winning horror film Weapons , which hit theaters last summer, and before that was his well-received Barbarian . Resident Evil reboots the film franchise adapting Capcom’s video game series that launched in 1996. The first live-action feature adaptation came with director Paul W.S. Anderson’s 2002 movie Resident Evil , with the Milla Jovovich-led project opening to $17.7 million domestically and going on to surpass $100 million globally throughout its run. Jovovich starred in five sequels before Kaya Scodelario led the 2021 reboot attempt Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City , which underperformed at the box office. Director Zach Cregger (right) and Austin Abrams on the set of Resident Evil. Dušan Martinček/Sony Pictures While the Resident Evil movies have not been known as critical darlings, the latest one is a very different story, as it holds an eye-popping 96 percent approval rating from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , critic Frank Scheck noted that Cregger “crafted a propulsive, simultaneously terrifying and hilarious thrill ride that showcases both his cinematic chops and perverse sense of humor.” As for Cregger, he told THR at the Los Angeles premiere that he had high hopes for the movie’s reception. “I felt pretty confident,” the director said. “We’ll see. Maybe I’m delusional, but I don’t think so. I’ve seen the movie, and I like it.” This should provide more of a jolt to the early days of fall than the previous frame, which saw Warner Bros.’ Practical Magic 2 take the top spot in a subdued debut that ended the six-weekend winning streak for Sony’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day . Earlier this week, the Tom Holland-led Spidey movie swung its way to No. 1 on the all-time domestic chart, toppling Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens . Unfortunately, the man without fear was already booked. “They told us we couldn’t have him because of [HBO’s live-action series] Lanterns , which I understood,” Zak Penn , one of the series’ creators, revealed to Deadline. “Chuck [Lorre] was a little grumbly about it, but Bill and I pointed out to him that Flash was actually perfect. If we needed something that’s going from dimension to dimension, Flash worked even better than Green Lantern.” Like Penn says, the episode ultimately sees Stuart (Kevin Sussman) and his friends stuck inside a comic book, where Mr. Freeze is terrorizing Gotham City. To get out of that dimension, they go off in search of Golden Age Flash for help. Watch on Deadline “It was half opportunity and half what they encouraged us, but Golden Age Flash appealed to us a lot, just because he’s kind of silly. No offense to Golden Age Flash,” Penn said. If it seems kind of backward that the gang would trek all the way to Central City to enlist The Flash to help them take on a villain in Batman’s territory, that’s the point. The writers reveled in the opportunity to poke fun at the more far-fetched notions accepted in comic lore. “Bill [Prady] and I were laughing a lot [about] the whole notion of Gotham City isn’t where New York City is, which makes no sense,” Penn said. “All those things were just kind of built up humor and things that we felt about comic books. So, the next obvious decision was, in terms of a villain, let’s put the villain who seems right and that people know more, and then have our characters comment on the fact that he’s the wrong villain for this piece.” Penn is surely considered the superhero expert of the group as a Marvel vet who also famously wrote a script for a Suicide Squad film that went unused. However, he says his fellow creators Prady and Lorre, as well as several of the other writers, had their own affinity for DC comics to draw upon for the episode. He and the writers thought a commentary on how a layperson would navigate a comic locale like Gotham City “seemed like the perfect sense of humor for our show.” “If you were in the DC universe, it would be pretty boring a lot of the time because you’d just be sitting around waiting for planes,” he laughs, adding that the irony is there’s also a bit about that exact notion in an early episode of Lanterns. That other DC show didn’t steal all Stuart ‘s thunder, though, and in fact there is plenty that the comedy series can get away with that its drama counterparts cannot in that the writers can lean into the quirks of these convoluted superhero universes rather than shy away. “One of the things about this show that’s really fun is that you know when you work on an actual comic book movie, you really have to be rigorous about the consistency of the reality, because people will pick you apart if you’re not, and on this show we kind of took the attitude of ‘we’re going to purposely break things and then have the characters notice that the multiverse doesn’t work as well as it should,'” Penn explained. Similarly, Penn says the episode could adopt a visual style more consistent with comic books without asking the audience to do more work suspending their disbelief. “[Director] Robbie McNeill deserves a lot of credit, because he really added a bunch of stuff, like the way the frames panel at certain points, which is something that I don’t always think is effective. Back in the early days of comic book movies, when people did that, I think it really took you out of it,” Penn told Deadline. “But this show’s sense of humor needs that, so it was really helpful.” The writers worked closely with DC’s Jim Lee to develop the versions of the comic characters that appear in Thursday’s episode. Lee teased the partnership over the summer at San Diego Comic-Con, assuring the audience in Hall H that the DC IP would be in good hands with the Stuart team. “Some of the DC characters they have in it, I think are some of the best versions I’ve seen of those characters, and so I’m super excited for you guys,” Lee said at the time. Penn, who had previously collaborated with Lee and the DC team on Ready Player One , remembered the Stuart reteam fondly: “They were great. They basically said, ‘How can we help? Other than we won’t give you Green Lantern.'” The series has already been renewed for a second season ahead of next week’s Season 1 finale. Penn tells Deadline he “would be shocked” if the writers didn’t once again mine from the DC universe in future episodes, but Season 2 is still in early stages. “The writers’ room hasn’t started yet. Next week, we’re going to get back together and start talking about this,” he said.
